# Step 1: Air Temperature vs. MRT

Start by exploring the difference between air temperature and MRT. Choose several observations from the dataset and compare AirT_C_detrended and MRT_C_detrended. • Are air temperature and MRT usually similar? • When are the differences largest? • Why can two locations with similar air temperatures have very different MRT? Use examples from the dataset in your explanation.

## Differences

```{r}
#| label: Create new variable 'diff'
#| include: false
marty$diff <- marty$MRT_C_detrended - marty$AirT_C_detrended
```

```{r}
#| label: Create histogram
#| include: true
hist_diff <- hist(marty$diff, right = FALSE, col = "firebrick", las = 1)
```

The histogram shows us that broadly, air temperature and MRT are fairly similar. The largest columns are all clustered around 0, meaning there are a lot of results with only a small difference between the two variables. However, there is also a small but noticeable cluster of results with a larger difference (around 20-40), showing that there are plenty of exceptions where the two values diverge.

## Linear Regression

```{r}
#| label: linear regression
#| include: true
# dependent variable: diff
# independent variables: Time_of_Day, Surface_Type, Shade_Category2

# build model
reg_diff <- lm(diff ~ Time_of_Day + Surface_Type + Shade_Category2, data = marty)

summary(reg_diff)
```

```{r}
#| label: ANOVA
#| include: true
anova(reg_diff)
```

Choose a visualization that helps answer the question and briefly explain what the figure shows. Your figure might illustrate average MRT by shade category, individual observations, MRT at different times of day, or another useful comparison. \# Step 3: Does Time of Day Matter?
